raw_response:
I have been growing chrysanthemum in Quzhou for four decades. I know this land and this crop deeply. My 35 mu is all chrysanthemum — that is what this county does well, and at my age, alone, I am not going to diversify and complicate things.

Spring is when I prepare. I will do rotary tillage first — chrysanthemum roots need loose, well-drained soil, and I have always done it this way. I use the improved local variety, not the old traditional cuts my father used, but not hybrid either. The improved Quzhou strains have better flower density and dry weight, which matters when I sell to the medicinal market.

Fertilizer: I apply more potassium than most younger farmers bother with because flower quality depends on it. I put down nitrogen at around 12 kg per mu — split between base and topdressing around branching stage. Phosphorus I keep moderate at 6 kg, potassium higher at 10 kg. Forty years of soil in this plot tells me this works.

Water: my well is reliable but electricity is not free. I irrigate six times — once at transplanting, twice through summer heat, then carefully spaced through bud and flower development. I do not over-water; chrysanthemum roots rot easily.

Pests and disease: aphids come every year, spider mites in July, and gray mold near harvest if the autumn is wet. I spray four times on a scheduled basis, adjusting if I see pressure. I know the signs.

Expected yield: around 120 kg of dried flos per mu. Consistent with what I have gotten the last several years.
